title: North American “warming holes” and European heat during abrupt Holocene cooling events in the Atlantic

paper_content.abstract: In recent decades, Europe has warmed rapidly while a prominent ‘warming hole’ has muted changes in eastern North America. Paradoxically, the pattern coincides with cooling in the North Atlantic, even though ocean cooling is commonly expected to chill Europe, not North America. The regional departures from global trends and expectations may have informative precedents in millennial-scale climate anomalies during the Holocene. Here, circum-Atlantic records reveal that counter-intuitive European warming developed amid rapid cooling of the North Atlantic and North America from 5.8-4.8 ka and after 2.2 ka. The anomalies track rapid reductions in the flow of North Atlantic Deep Water southwest of Iceland and appear in independent but highly correlated records of mean sea-surface temperatures, continental temperatures, and hydroclimate changes from both sides of the Atlantic. The patterns confirm the importance of millennial climate variability during the Holocene and the risk of climate disruptions around the North Atlantic today.
paper_content.introduction:
As current anthropogenic climate trends increase the risk of rapid climatic state shifts, unusual patterns such as ‘warming holes,’ intense heatwaves, and extreme droughts differentiate regional responses1–5 (Fig. 1). The patterns of interglacial climates may provide useful analogs for understanding such regional departures from global trends6,7. Looking beyond the slow, globalevolution of Holocene climates can reveal controls on abrupt shifts and regional differences possible during warm Earth system states8. Holocene climate changes were likely part of a power-law spectrum of variability, including significant millennial variability, particularly at regional scales7,9. Mismatches between paleoclimate reconstructions and orbitally-forced Holocene climate simulations underscore the need to re-examine any potential millennial-scale dynamics10,11 by identifying and evaluating benchmark patterns useful for testing numerical and conceptual models12,13.

The challenge is not simply recognizing that millennial changes took place during the Holocene, but rather to develop synoptic perspectives aimed at predicting their spatial patterns, regional impacts, and implications for the future. To do so, we examine a geographically gridded network of pollen-inferred summer warmth reconstructions, representing growing degree days above 5°C (GDD5)13, as well as an updated network of sea-surface temperature (SST) reconstructions spanning the North Atlantic Ocean. The SST reconstructions, updated from the Temp12ka dataset14, include all available reconstructions from 8.0–0.8 ka to maximize geographic coverage. We use the data to evaluate correlations among continental climates and broad oceanic changes within the western and central North Atlantic, although sparse data coverage prevents analyses of some relevant spatial patterns, such as those directly related to the Gulf Stream15.

Here, the network of records allows us to study millennial climate variations that were sufficiently large and extensive to coordinate impacts in disjunct ecosystems across two continents. We examine the hypotheses that interglacial instability affected North Atlantic climates and that North Atlantic cooling, such as that induced by slowed Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), can chill Europe amid a globally warm climate. Models are uncertain about such risks during interglacial climates12,16. We focus on summer patterns of the past 8 ka after the influence of the northern hemisphere ice sheets diminished and find patterns consistent with current North Atlantic cooling, the summer ‘warming hole’ in North America, coincident extreme heat in Europe, and affiliated hydroclimate changes (Fig. 1).
paper_content.results:
Opposite sign millennial changes in Europe and North America Summer temperature (GDD5) changes over the past 8000 years include millennia with different direction anomalies across northwest Europe and mid-latitude eastern North America (ENA; Fig. 2). Over the long term, summer warmth declined across northwest Europe (orange line, Fig. 2A) and, to a lesser degree, mid-latitude ENA (blue line, Fig. 2A). Previous work showed that a stepwise increase in temperature interrupted the trends in the mid-Holocene13. However, the mid-Holocene increase developed primarily in Europe as ENA cooled from 5.8-4.8 ka (blue bar, Fig. 2A). Abrupt warming in Europe and cooling in ENA was then repeated at 2.2 ka (gray bars, Fig. 2A). Both events increased the thermal difference between the continents in summer.

The changes after 2.2 ka warmed Europe but cooled ENA and the North Atlantic during the Roman Warm Period (RWP) and Medieval Climate Anomaly (MCA), demonstrating large-scale reorganization but not universal warmth17.

Mean SSTs across the central and western North Atlantic declined rapidly as Europe warmed at 5.8 and 2.2 ka (black line, Fig. 2B). The mean rate of central-western SST change (from southwest of Iceland to the Gulf of Mexico, as defined by the large inset box in Fig. 2D, E) correlates negatively with the European rate of GDD5 change per millennium (Fig. 2C; Pearson product moment correlation, r = −0.39, 95% CI: −0.58 - −0.15, df=61). Maps show expansive North Atlantic cooling, as well as warming like that today (Fig. 1C) west of Greenland and along the Labrador coast (Fig. 2D). Linear regression indicates that for every 1°C of cooling in the central-western North Atlantic mean, northwest European warmth increases by the equivalent of 1°C over ~100 days per year: ΔGDD5 = (−101±28°C days °C SST −1xΔSST) - 31±7°C days where Δ represent the rate of change per 1000 years (adjusted R2=0.16, df=61, p=0.0006). Other analyses of SSTs affirm the rapid mid-Holocene cooling8,18,19, although individual records commonly differ from the means because of spatial variability typical of the surface ocean.

The temperature changes after 5.8 and 2.2 ka also correspond to effective moisture changes (Figs. 3, 4), which are spatially similar to those that exist today (Fig. 1). The oceanic changes (Fig. 3A, B) and reduced ENA temperatures (Fig. 3C) correlate significantly with an increase in mean effective moisture across ENA (increased lake levels, reduced dust, Fig. 3D)20. The increase likely facilitated cooling there by reducing sensible heating2 (Fig. 3C). Reduced effective moisture may have produced the opposite outcome in other regions, such as California (Fig. 3D) and Europe (Fig. 4). Trees submerged in Sierra Nevada lakes have been interpreted as evidence of severe droughts in California from 5.8–4.5 ka and after 2.2 ka21,22 (histogram, Fig. 3D). From 4.8–3.5 ka, the reverse hydroclimate pattern developed with drying common in ENA20 (Fig. 3D) and sedimentary evidence of pluvial conditions in the Sierra Nevada23. Likewise, a previous synthesis of lake-level records from Europe24 indicates a strong correlation between summer warmth and effective moisture (Fig. 4A, B; Pearson product-moment correlation, r=-0.77, 95% CI: −0.88 - −0.60, df=35). Low effective moisture extended furthest across Europe during peak warmth from 5.8–4.6 ka. Afterwards, lakes rose widely except during renewed warming and drying from 2.2–1.4 ka (Fig. 4B). The correlations among European and North American temperature changes (Fig. 2A), with North Atlantic SSTs (Fig. 3B, C), and with the sedimentary evidence of hydroclimate changes (Figs. 3, 4) show no significant lags in the pollen response underlying the temperature reconstructions and indicating rapid terrestrial ecosystem consequences.

Context of AMOC reorganization

The millennial temperature anomalies during the Holocene appear related to AMOC reorganization, even if a large-scale shutdown did not take place (blue bar, Fig. 3). North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) flow rates declined, at least in some areas, when much of the North Atlantic Ocean cooled (Fig. 3A, B). The flow rate inferred from the mean size of sortable silt from southwest of Iceland25 (core MD2251, Fig. 3A) correlates significantly with our mean SST reconstruction (Figs. 2B, 3B) (Pearson product moment correlation, r=0.78, 95% CI: 0.67–0.86, df=61). The correlation exceeds the 95% range of 1000 random surrogate time series with the same spectral properties (see Supplementary Information) and suggests that the MD2251 record could represent a broad North Atlantic dynamic. The detailed sortable silt record from core MD225125 linearly predicts not only the mean SST history (Fig. 3B) but also changes in North American temperature and hydroclimate (Fig. 3C, D) and the timing of the GDD5 changes in northwest Europe (Fig. 4).

Other mineralogical indicators of NADW flow26 and an additional set of sortable silt records from near Iceland27 confirm the correlation with SSTs (Fig. 5A, B) expressed in core MD2251 (Fig. 3A). They indicate that Iceland-Scotland (I-S) overflow, a component of the AMOC, slowed at 5.8 and 2.2 ka, especially at water depths of <1.6 km27, even though overflow flow remained persistently high elsewhere28,29 (see Supplementary Information). The continuous flow rates in these other areas agree with 231Pa/230Th records that indicate negligible Holocene changes in deep-water residence times30. However, carbon isotopes show limited NADW penetration near Bermuda31 and Ireland32 from 5.8–4.8 ka (see Supplementary Information). Changes afterwards involved a rapid acceleration of Labrador Sea Water flow, another component of AMOC, off eastern Canada33. The AMOC flow signals appear reproducible (Fig. 5B), but dependent on location, which reveals spatial variability and Holocene proxy differences tied to diverging flow, penetration, and residence time variations, which have analogs in variability among sites and proxies during Pleistocene abrupt changes34 and today35.
paper_content.methods:
Modern climate trends
Maps of modern climate trends around the North Atlantic Ocean (Fig. 1) were generated using the NCAR/NCEP Reanalysis I56. The differences between CE 1951–2000 and 2001–2020 were calculated using online tools provided by the NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, Colorado, USA, and obtained as NetCDF files from their website at https://psl.noaa.gov/. The focus on 21st century differences from the second half of the 20th century avoids effects of the warm, dry CE 1930s on the ‘warming hole’ and related North American temperature statistics2,4,5.

Holocene temperatures
The 2°x2° latitude/longitude grid of growing degree day base 5°C (GDD5) reconstructions from Marsicek et al.13 were extracted from the NOAA Paleoclimate database (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/paleo-search/study/22992) and mapped using R version 4.3.157. The reconstructions include 100-year time steps spanning the Holocene based on GDD5 reconstructions from 584 pollen records that passed a significance screen based on comparisons of each reconstruction with a distribution of random null models for each site13. We map the changes for the 5.8 and 4.8 ka intervals (Fig. 2) as well as 2.2 ka (Fig. SI2) based on the change over 600 years by subtracting an initial interval (6.0, 5.3, or 2.5 ka) from a post-change interval (5.4, 4.9, or 1.9 ka, respectively). The changes were mapped after classifying the anomalies into zero change (−50 to 50°C days), moderate change (50–100°C days magnitude) and large changes (>100°C days magnitude).

To produce European and North American GDD5 timeseries, grid cells from the target regions were extracted and averaged per century. For each century, beginning at 9 ka, 75% of the available grid cells in each region were randomly selected and averaged using base functions in R. The process was repeated 100 times to generate a distribution of mean GDD5 reconstructions for each region, which accounts for spatial variability and differences in time and reconstruction uncertainty among the grid cells13; the timeseries in Fig. 2A show the median and 95% range of the regional means. The CE 1950 (0 ka) value was subtracted from each of the regional means prior to plotting as anomalies. GDD5 units represent the mean annual sum of degree days, which are total daily mean increases in degrees (°C or K) above 5°C per year.

To produce timeseries of North Atlantic Ocean sea-surface temperatures (SSTs), all SST reconstructions from the Temp12ka database14 were combined with additional SST reconstructions from the region that spanned from 8.0–0.9 ka43,58–60 (Table SI1). The additional records were either too new or did not span a sufficient duration of the Holocene for inclusion in the Temp12ka dataset. All data were obtained from either the PANGAEA or NOAA Paleoclimate databases, and most derived from two sources: Temperature 12ka Database (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-020-0445-3)14 and the database of Holocene temperature reconstructions for northeastern North America and the northwestern Atlantic (https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.905293)58. Additional individual records were then identified and added43,59,60.

For consistency with the GDD5 data, each SST record was interpolated to 100-yr time steps using base functions in R in accordance with recommendations61. Maps show their differences based on the same 600-yr time intervals as used for the GDD5 data. Likewise, all SST reconstructions from southwest of Iceland to the Gulf of Mexico (south of 65°N and west of 15°W) were averaged using the same iterative approach, based on 100 iterations of 75% of the records to create a mean SST timeseries and 95% confidence interval. The CE 1950 (0 ka) value was again subtracted from the mean prior to plotting as anomalies. To confirm the spatial extent and coherence of the anomalies, the same approach was used with the prcomp function in R to conduct a principal components analysis (PCA), except that all 77 SST records spanning from 8.0–0.9 ka north of 20°N were included (Fig. SI3). All SST reconstructions were included regardless of seasonality to ensure maximum geographic coverage and because the magnitudes of millennial anomalies are consistent across seasons, but the Supplementary Information includes versions of the analysis using only annual (Fig. SI1, n=26 in our core study region) and only summer SST reconstructions (Fig. SI2, n=7 in our core study region).

Rates of change and correlations
Rates of change (Fig. 2C) were calculated by subtracting the change in the regional mean GDD5 and SST reconstructions over 1000-year intervals, centered on the 500-year mid-point for each interval. Time series in Fig. 3 compare our mean SST and the previously published a) NADW flow rate reconstruction based on sortable silt size data from core MD2251 from the central Gardar Drift, south of Iceland25, b) eastern North America mean temperature of the warmest month (MTWM) reconstruction based on well-resolved fossil pollen stratigraphies between Wyoming and Maine20, and c) eastern North America mean effective moisture based on the average z-scores of dust and lake-level records from Wyoming to Massachusetts20. The correlations of the NADW flow rate with the SST, MTWM, and moisture reconstructions were compared with those calculated based on 1000 random surrogate time series with a power-law spectrum with the same spectral slope as the actual reconstructions; the surrogates were generated and correlations compared using the corit package in R61. The correlations were compared based on both the raw (Fig. SI4) and detrended timeseries (see Fig. SI5). To compare the different sign GDD5 changes in Europe and North America, the absolute values of the 1000-yr rates of change were also compared (Fig. SI6).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Shuman and Stefanescu makes some interesting observations about broad-scale patterns of temperature and hydroclimate change between North America, Europe, and the North Atlantic during the Holocene. They make a fairly compelling case that there are two times when these regions shift in relative directions that are broadly consistent with patterns of change during recent decades: at ~5.8 and 2.2 ka, Europe warmed, eastern North America cooled and got wetter, the western US dried, and SSTs cooled. I am supportive of eventual publication, but I have some substantial comments that should be addressed in revision.
One weakness is that the ocean fingerprint over recent decades, that of a ‘warming hole’ southwest of Iceland, cannot really be resolved with present paleo-SST data. Instead the authors combine the entire North Atlantic south and west of Iceland, for which “southwest of Iceland” is a misleading name (the box is referred to as black in the Fig 2 caption, but I think it’s the giant gray box). In attributing the modern SST pattern to an AMOC slowdown, the region of extreme warming off the northeast US is equally important, as it plausibly reflects the accumulation of Gulf Stream heat there. The paleo data do not show such a dipole (Fig 2D), though warming off west Greenland and east Labrador fits. I suggest that the authors explicitly acknowledge the limitations of the paleo SST data, particularly the lack of coverage in the modern Gulf Stream warming region, and that the data is overall too sparse to clearly reconstruct spatial patterns. Here a spatial infilling technique could be valuable, but that could be left to future work.
The subject of paleo AMOC as an explanation is really key to this paper, but the lede is kind of buried, because AMOC does not appear in the title or the abstract. The comparison in Fig 3 of the sortable silt record to regional records (SST, ENA temperature, ENA moisture) is quite striking. I would guess that the authors’ reticence is related to the fact that other sortable silt records from the region show different patterns (e.g. the gray line in Fig 4). Thornalley et al. (2013, Clim Past) do a nice job of showing that Holocene SS is reproducible, but highly dependent on which part of NADW the core sits in. I encourage the authors to provide a fuller context here, and talk about what, exactly, the Hoogaaker record likely records, relative to other records that show different histories. I believe Thornalley commented on that issue. He also provided a weighted ISOW stack that, although low resolution, shows a slowdown around 6 ka. It’s not clear why the authors show the gray record in Fig 4 rather than other options. The idea of ISOW compensating for LSW (p. 9) left me confused in terms of both supporting evidence and whether it is required.
I’m not sure how the Florida Straits SST record in Figure 4 fits in: is it recording AMOC strength directly (northward flow of tropical waters)? The new Florida Straits O2 record is also mentioned as fitting the story, but I think the Holocene resolution and noise of that record is too poor to say anything.
I think the Discussion falls a bit flat on the question of forcing. Arguably we have an AMOC slowdown with continental climate effects that resemble the pattern over recent decades. That would both strengthen the idea that the recent warming hole is due to AMOC, and that the continental patterns may be too. Again, a bit buried. But why did this all happen? Is it stochastic? The coincidental timing of the end of the African Humid Period is intriguing. That event has been interpreted as a positive feedback threshold response to slow orbital forcing. Might the same idea play out on AMOC? Or was the AMOC a response to AHP-related changes in hydroclimate?
In Fig 1B, why has the air over the warming Gulf Stream (off northeastern US) actually cooled?
I may have missed it, but are there European paleo-hydroclimate indicators that might fit the strong pattern shown in Fig 1C? If there are indicators but they are ambiguous or don’t ffit, that should be briefly mentioned.
The nature of the SST proxies should be briefly mentioned in the introduction, and not left solely to the Methods. The reference numbers in Table S1 don’t seem to match the Methods or the reference list.
I found the labels on Fig 2D-E confusing. I suggest changing them to “5.4 minus 6.0 ka” and “4.7 minus 5.3 ka.”
Second line of abstract: remove “also.”
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript by Shuman and Stefanescu presents a novel spatial analysis of Holocene climate anomalies of the last 8000 years. As the authors indicate, this analysis is urgently required for drawing lessons of relevance from the Holocene past for ongoing and future climate changes linked to the dynamics of the Atlantic system. The study builds on an existing pollen database that underpinned previous reconstructions through Holocene time, but presents the original findings of spatial analysis for N America and Europe, coupled to new analysis of palaeoceanographic records for the Atlantic. Overall, it is a powerful approach that permits a robust comparison across the Atlantic sector, with noteworthy detection of contrasting temperature anomalies between the regions. The methodology is sound, evidencing careful attention to statistical analysis of correlations between different records. The results are noteworthy and can provide a stimulus for the research community to consider the spatial component of Holocene climate changes in more detail. Overall, I would recommend publication of this manuscript with attention to some line-by-line detailed comments and some more general observations (>>) given below, generally with some attention to strengthening the final discussion.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

In recent decades, Europe has warmed rapidly while a prominent ‘warming hole’ has muted changes in eastern North America. Paradoxically, the pattern coincides with cooling in the North Atlantic, even though ocean cooling is commonly expected to chill Europe, not North America. The regional departures from global trends and expectations may have informative precedents in millennial-scale climate anomalies during the Holocene. Here, circum-Atlantic records reveal that counter-intuitive European warming developed amid rapid cooling of the North Atlantic and North America from 5.8-4.8 ka and after 2.2 ka. The anomalies track rapid reductions in the flow of North Atlantic Deep Water southwest of Iceland and appear in independent but highly correlated records of mean sea-surface temperatures, continental temperatures, and hydroclimate changes from both sides of the Atlantic. The patterns confirm the importance of millennial climate variability during the Holocene and the risk of climate disruptions around the North Atlantic today.

---

## Introduction

As current anthropogenic climate trends increase the risk of rapid climatic state shifts, unusual patterns such as ‘warming holes,’ intense heatwaves, and extreme droughts differentiate regional responses1–5 (Fig. 1). The patterns of interglacial climates may provide useful analogs for understanding such regional departures from global trends6,7. Looking beyond the slow, globalevolution of Holocene climates can reveal controls on abrupt shifts and regional differences possible during warm Earth system states8. Holocene climate changes were likely part of a power-law spectrum of variability, including significant millennial variability, particularly at regional scales7,9. Mismatches between paleoclimate reconstructions and orbitally-forced Holocene climate simulations underscore the need to re-examine any potential millennial-scale dynamics10,11 by identifying and evaluating benchmark patterns useful for testing numerical and conceptual models12,13.

The challenge is not simply recognizing that millennial changes took place during the Holocene, but rather to develop synoptic perspectives aimed at predicting their spatial patterns, regional impacts, and implications for the future. To do so, we examine a geographically gridded network of pollen-inferred summer warmth reconstructions, representing growing degree days above 5°C (GDD5)13, as well as an updated network of sea-surface temperature (SST) reconstructions spanning the North Atlantic Ocean. The SST reconstructions, updated from the Temp12ka dataset14, include all available reconstructions from 8.0–0.8 ka to maximize geographic coverage. We use the data to evaluate correlations among continental climates and broad oceanic changes within the western and central North Atlantic, although sparse data coverage prevents analyses of some relevant spatial patterns, such as those directly related to the Gulf Stream15.

Here, the network of records allows us to study millennial climate variations that were sufficiently large and extensive to coordinate impacts in disjunct ecosystems across two continents. We examine the hypotheses that interglacial instability affected North Atlantic climates and that North Atlantic cooling, such as that induced by slowed Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), can chill Europe amid a globally warm climate. Models are uncertain about such risks during interglacial climates12,16. We focus on summer patterns of the past 8 ka after the influence of the northern hemisphere ice sheets diminished and find patterns consistent with current North Atlantic cooling, the summer ‘warming hole’ in North America, coincident extreme heat in Europe, and affiliated hydroclimate changes (Fig. 1).

---

## Results

Opposite sign millennial changes in Europe and North America Summer temperature (GDD5) changes over the past 8000 years include millennia with different direction anomalies across northwest Europe and mid-latitude eastern North America (ENA; Fig. 2). Over the long term, summer warmth declined across northwest Europe (orange line, Fig. 2A) and, to a lesser degree, mid-latitude ENA (blue line, Fig. 2A). Previous work showed that a stepwise increase in temperature interrupted the trends in the mid-Holocene13. However, the mid-Holocene increase developed primarily in Europe as ENA cooled from 5.8-4.8 ka (blue bar, Fig. 2A). Abrupt warming in Europe and cooling in ENA was then repeated at 2.2 ka (gray bars, Fig. 2A). Both events increased the thermal difference between the continents in summer.

The changes after 2.2 ka warmed Europe but cooled ENA and the North Atlantic during the Roman Warm Period (RWP) and Medieval Climate Anomaly (MCA), demonstrating large-scale reorganization but not universal warmth17.

Mean SSTs across the central and western North Atlantic declined rapidly as Europe warmed at 5.8 and 2.2 ka (black line, Fig. 2B). The mean rate of central-western SST change (from southwest of Iceland to the Gulf of Mexico, as defined by the large inset box in Fig. 2D, E) correlates negatively with the European rate of GDD5 change per millennium (Fig. 2C; Pearson product moment correlation, r = −0.39, 95% CI: −0.58 - −0.15, df=61). Maps show expansive North Atlantic cooling, as well as warming like that today (Fig. 1C) west of Greenland and along the Labrador coast (Fig. 2D). Linear regression indicates that for every 1°C of cooling in the central-western North Atlantic mean, northwest European warmth increases by the equivalent of 1°C over ~100 days per year: ΔGDD5 = (−101±28°C days °C SST −1xΔSST) - 31±7°C days where Δ represent the rate of change per 1000 years (adjusted R2=0.16, df=61, p=0.0006). Other analyses of SSTs affirm the rapid mid-Holocene cooling8,18,19, although individual records commonly differ from the means because of spatial variability typical of the surface ocean.

The temperature changes after 5.8 and 2.2 ka also correspond to effective moisture changes (Figs. 3, 4), which are spatially similar to those that exist today (Fig. 1). The oceanic changes (Fig. 3A, B) and reduced ENA temperatures (Fig. 3C) correlate significantly with an increase in mean effective moisture across ENA (increased lake levels, reduced dust, Fig. 3D)20. The increase likely facilitated cooling there by reducing sensible heating2 (Fig. 3C). Reduced effective moisture may have produced the opposite outcome in other regions, such as California (Fig. 3D) and Europe (Fig. 4). Trees submerged in Sierra Nevada lakes have been interpreted as evidence of severe droughts in California from 5.8–4.5 ka and after 2.2 ka21,22 (histogram, Fig. 3D). From 4.8–3.5 ka, the reverse hydroclimate pattern developed with drying common in ENA20 (Fig. 3D) and sedimentary evidence of pluvial conditions in the Sierra Nevada23. Likewise, a previous synthesis of lake-level records from Europe24 indicates a strong correlation between summer warmth and effective moisture (Fig. 4A, B; Pearson product-moment correlation, r=-0.77, 95% CI: −0.88 - −0.60, df=35). Low effective moisture extended furthest across Europe during peak warmth from 5.8–4.6 ka. Afterwards, lakes rose widely except during renewed warming and drying from 2.2–1.4 ka (Fig. 4B). The correlations among European and North American temperature changes (Fig. 2A), with North Atlantic SSTs (Fig. 3B, C), and with the sedimentary evidence of hydroclimate changes (Figs. 3, 4) show no significant lags in the pollen response underlying the temperature reconstructions and indicating rapid terrestrial ecosystem consequences.

Context of AMOC reorganization

The millennial temperature anomalies during the Holocene appear related to AMOC reorganization, even if a large-scale shutdown did not take place (blue bar, Fig. 3). North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) flow rates declined, at least in some areas, when much of the North Atlantic Ocean cooled (Fig. 3A, B). The flow rate inferred from the mean size of sortable silt from southwest of Iceland25 (core MD2251, Fig. 3A) correlates significantly with our mean SST reconstruction (Figs. 2B, 3B) (Pearson product moment correlation, r=0.78, 95% CI: 0.67–0.86, df=61). The correlation exceeds the 95% range of 1000 random surrogate time series with the same spectral properties (see Supplementary Information) and suggests that the MD2251 record could represent a broad North Atlantic dynamic. The detailed sortable silt record from core MD225125 linearly predicts not only the mean SST history (Fig. 3B) but also changes in North American temperature and hydroclimate (Fig. 3C, D) and the timing of the GDD5 changes in northwest Europe (Fig. 4).

Other mineralogical indicators of NADW flow26 and an additional set of sortable silt records from near Iceland27 confirm the correlation with SSTs (Fig. 5A, B) expressed in core MD2251 (Fig. 3A). They indicate that Iceland-Scotland (I-S) overflow, a component of the AMOC, slowed at 5.8 and 2.2 ka, especially at water depths of <1.6 km27, even though overflow flow remained persistently high elsewhere28,29 (see Supplementary Information). The continuous flow rates in these other areas agree with 231Pa/230Th records that indicate negligible Holocene changes in deep-water residence times30. However, carbon isotopes show limited NADW penetration near Bermuda31 and Ireland32 from 5.8–4.8 ka (see Supplementary Information). Changes afterwards involved a rapid acceleration of Labrador Sea Water flow, another component of AMOC, off eastern Canada33. The AMOC flow signals appear reproducible (Fig. 5B), but dependent on location, which reveals spatial variability and Holocene proxy differences tied to diverging flow, penetration, and residence time variations, which have analogs in variability among sites and proxies during Pleistocene abrupt changes34 and today35.

---

## Methods

Modern climate trends
Maps of modern climate trends around the North Atlantic Ocean (Fig. 1) were generated using the NCAR/NCEP Reanalysis I56. The differences between CE 1951–2000 and 2001–2020 were calculated using online tools provided by the NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory, Boulder, Colorado, USA, and obtained as NetCDF files from their website at https://psl.noaa.gov/. The focus on 21st century differences from the second half of the 20th century avoids effects of the warm, dry CE 1930s on the ‘warming hole’ and related North American temperature statistics2,4,5.

Holocene temperatures
The 2°x2° latitude/longitude grid of growing degree day base 5°C (GDD5) reconstructions from Marsicek et al.13 were extracted from the NOAA Paleoclimate database (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/paleo-search/study/22992) and mapped using R version 4.3.157. The reconstructions include 100-year time steps spanning the Holocene based on GDD5 reconstructions from 584 pollen records that passed a significance screen based on comparisons of each reconstruction with a distribution of random null models for each site13. We map the changes for the 5.8 and 4.8 ka intervals (Fig. 2) as well as 2.2 ka (Fig. SI2) based on the change over 600 years by subtracting an initial interval (6.0, 5.3, or 2.5 ka) from a post-change interval (5.4, 4.9, or 1.9 ka, respectively). The changes were mapped after classifying the anomalies into zero change (−50 to 50°C days), moderate change (50–100°C days magnitude) and large changes (>100°C days magnitude).

To produce European and North American GDD5 timeseries, grid cells from the target regions were extracted and averaged per century. For each century, beginning at 9 ka, 75% of the available grid cells in each region were randomly selected and averaged using base functions in R. The process was repeated 100 times to generate a distribution of mean GDD5 reconstructions for each region, which accounts for spatial variability and differences in time and reconstruction uncertainty among the grid cells13; the timeseries in Fig. 2A show the median and 95% range of the regional means. The CE 1950 (0 ka) value was subtracted from each of the regional means prior to plotting as anomalies. GDD5 units represent the mean annual sum of degree days, which are total daily mean increases in degrees (°C or K) above 5°C per year.

To produce timeseries of North Atlantic Ocean sea-surface temperatures (SSTs), all SST reconstructions from the Temp12ka database14 were combined with additional SST reconstructions from the region that spanned from 8.0–0.9 ka43,58–60 (Table SI1). The additional records were either too new or did not span a sufficient duration of the Holocene for inclusion in the Temp12ka dataset. All data were obtained from either the PANGAEA or NOAA Paleoclimate databases, and most derived from two sources: Temperature 12ka Database (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-020-0445-3)14 and the database of Holocene temperature reconstructions for northeastern North America and the northwestern Atlantic (https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.905293)58. Additional individual records were then identified and added43,59,60.
